children: India needs to move beyond high-volume electronics assembly and strengthen product design, component manufacturing as well as intellectual property ownership to increase domestic value addition, panellists at Semicon  India 2026 said.

Speaking during a discussion on ‘Large-Scale Manufacturing: Paving the Path for Deeper Domestic Value Addition’, industry executives identified import dependence, manufacturing quality and skills gaps as challenges to scaling up production.

On its part, Tata Electronics’ Ranganathan V, Business Head, Products Group (FATP), said Indian companies needed to participate earlier in product design, as decisions on component selection and suppliers were often finalised before manufacturers became involved.
He highlighted the need for larger investments in automation to support the industry’s manufacturing ambitions.
Similarly, Rajendra Velagapudi, Managing Director and CEO, Cyient DLM, identified dependence on imported electronic components as a major supply chain concern.

He called for technology partnerships and joint ventures to strengthen local capabilities, while stressing the need for Indian companies to move towards design-led manufacturing and develop their own intellectual property.
Besides, Resolute Chairman and Managing Director Raminder Singh Soin called for national manufacturing quality benchmarks, with incentives linked to companies’ performance.
He said production yields needed to reach global standards, identifying process maturity and quality control as essential to manufacturing for export markets.
Soin identified local component production as an opportunity to raise domestic value addition to 40–50 per cent or higher.
He pointed to capacitors and resistors as areas where smaller enterprises could participate.

According to Pallavi Verma, Executive Director, Guidance Tamil Nadu, India needed to shift towards high-value manufacturing and address gaps in materials and the processing of rare earths and critical minerals.

Meanwhile, Siemens’ Aditya Ramakrishna said digital twins, which allow factories to be designed and simulated virtually, could help India shorten project timelines and reduce errors before committing large investments.
He said Siemens had helped a supplier in Taiwan reduce plant setup and commissioning time by around 20–30 per cent.
Furthermore, Ramakrishna identified software-defined automation as an emerging opportunity to help manufacturers adapt production systems as product development cycles become progressively shorter.
On skills, Ranganathan sought closer collaboration with universities, greater research activity and engineering programmes aligned with industrial applications.
In addition, Verma called for industry and academic institutions to work together to bridge the gap between engineering education and employers’ requirements.

title: India must move beyond electronics assembly: Industry
